Just now

--

I’ve given a lot of interviews. Google, Amazon, Qualcomm, Telus — I’ve written about most of them. After a while you feel like you’ve seen it all: the coding round, the project questions, the “explain YOLO” round, the behavioral stuff. You kind of know what’s coming.
Then Toshiba asked me things I did not see coming at all.
This is the story of the interview that reminded me I’d stopped studying the one thing every AI engineer thinks they know by heart — the math behind the models. Two days later I got the rejection email. But this one taught me more than some of the interviews I actually passed.
Press enter or click to view image in full size

It started off totally normal
The interview was for an AI Engineer role and lasted about 40 minutes. It began the way these things usually do — a friendly intro, some small talk about my background. Easy. Nothing to worry about.
Then he asked me to walk him through one of my recent projects, and I relaxed even more, because this is my favorite part. Talking about real work I’ve done, on real systems — that’s where I’m strongest. We went deep. He asked lots of follow-up questions about the choices I made and the problems I ran into. I felt good. This was my comfort zone.
If the interview had ended right there, I’d have walked out sure that I nailed it.
Then he said, “let’s do some math”
And some turned out to be a big word.
He started easy. Cross product and dot product — no problem, I know these. I answered fine and thought, okay, just warming up.
It was not just warming up.
Next came linear regression — write it out, explain it. Still okay. Then logistic regression — how it works, why we use the sigmoid, how it’s different from linear regression. I was still hanging on, but I could feel the ground getting shakier under me.
Then he said it: “Let’s talk about gradient descent.”
This is where I got uncomfortable
Here’s the honest part, and the whole reason I’m writing this instead of pretending it went great.
I use gradient descent all the time. Every model I’ve ever trained runs on it. I can tell you what it does, why it matters, what a learning rate is. But when he asked me to actually work through the math behind it — live, on the spot — I wasn’t ready. I hadn’t touched that math in a long time. In everyday work you just call .backward() and the framework handles it for you. You stop thinking about how the engine works because the car keeps driving fine without you looking.
I wasn’t expecting this much math in an AI interview. I’ve done many of them, and no one had ever gone this deep into the basics. Everyone else wanted to know if I could build things. Toshiba wanted to know if I really understood why the things I build actually work.
I answered what I could. I wasn’t confident, and I’m pretty sure it showed.
And then, a tree question
After the math, he switched to a DSA question about trees — back to friendlier ground. But by then the gradient descent part had shaken me a little, and once your confidence takes a hit mid-interview, it’s hard to fully bounce back.
Forty minutes, done. I walked away knowing I hadn’t answered everything the way I wanted to. Two days later, the rejection email said the same thing.
What this interview taught me
I’ve thought about this one more than some interviews I passed, because it showed me a real gap — not just a bad day.
Frameworks make you good and rusty at the same time. PyTorch and TensorFlow are amazing. But they’ve also quietly let a lot of us forget the math they’re built on. I can deploy a shrunk-down model to a tiny edge device, but I froze on the math behind gradient descent. Both are true. Only one of them shows up in an interview like this.
Not every company is testing the same thing. Most AI interviews I’d done were about engineering — can you build it, can you ship it, can you deploy it. Toshiba was about the basics — do you understand the machine at the level of its math. Neither is wrong. But you need to know which kind of room you’re walking into. I walked into a “basics” room dressed for a “systems” interview.
“I use it every day” is not the same as “I can explain the math right now.” This one is a trap for experienced people especially. The more senior you get, the more you work at a high level — and the further you drift from the equations you learned years ago. Some companies will happily ask you to climb back down and explain the fundamentals, step by step.
What I’d tell you if you’re interviewing for AI roles
Go back and revise the basics. Not just for Toshiba — for any company that might test them. And don’t just be able to describe these things, be able to actually work through them:

• Dot product and cross product, and why they matter in ML

• Linear regression from scratch

• Logistic regression and why the sigmoid is there

• Gradient descent — the actual math, not just “it goes downhill.” Know the update rule, what the gradient is doing, what the learning rate does, and be able to talk through it out loud.
If you can build models but you’d freeze trying to explain the math behind them — well, that was me two days before this interview. Fix it before a company finds out for you.
No hard feelings
I didn’t get the offer, but I’m honestly kind of glad this one happened. It found a real weak spot that all my building-and-deploying experience had been nicely hiding. I’ve been going back over the basics ever since — not to chase Toshiba, but because the interview had a point. I should be able to explain the tools I use every single day.
Rejections are data, not a final verdict. This one told me exactly what to study next. That’s worth more than a polite “we’ll keep your resume on file.”
If you’ve got a Toshiba-style interview coming up: study your math. All of it. They’re not bluffing.
